forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, l with 0 ≤ k, l ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.

forbidden_claims.statement_nl: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0. Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Let S be the weighted polynomial ring Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i) = B+i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Equivalently, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in a weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.

payload.previous_proof_nl:
Let K be an algebraic closure of k and set J := I*K[x_1,...,x_d] inside K[x_1,...,x_d]. The hypothesis says that the common zero set of J in K^d is exactly {0}.

If d = 0, then S = k. The affine 0-space over K has one point, the origin. Since the zero locus of I is that point, I is not the unit ideal; hence I = 0. Therefore S/I is k itself, so it is finite-dimensional over k.

Now assume d >= 1. By Hilbert's Nullstellensatz over the algebraically closed field K, rad(J) is the ideal of all polynomials vanishing at {0}, namely m0 := (x_1,...,x_d). Thus for each i there exists N_i >= 1 with x_i^{N_i} in J.

We claim that J intersect S = I. The inclusion I subset J intersect S is obvious. For the reverse inclusion, let f be in J intersect S. Since f is in J, we can write
f = sum_{r=1}^M A_r f_r
with A_r in K[x_1,...,x_d] and f_r in I.
Let V be the k-subspace of K spanned by 1 and by all coefficients of all A_r. This V is finite-dimensional. Choose a k-basis 1 = beta_1, beta_2, ..., beta_t of V. Then each A_r can be written as
A_r = sum_{s=1}^t beta_s B_{r,s}
with B_{r,s} in S.
Hence
f = sum_{r,s} beta_s B_{r,s} f_r = sum_{s=1}^t beta_s G_s,
where G_s := sum_r B_{r,s} f_r belongs to I.
Set H_1 := G_1 - f and H_s := G_s for s > 1. Then
beta_1 H_1 + beta_2 H_2 + ... + beta_t H_t = 0.
Write H_s = sum_alpha c_{s,alpha} x^alpha with c_{s,alpha} in k. For each monomial x^alpha, the coefficient of x^alpha in the displayed relation is
sum_{s=1}^t beta_s c_{s,alpha} = 0.
Since beta_1,...,beta_t are k-linearly independent, all c_{s,alpha} are 0. So every H_s is 0, hence G_1 = f and G_s = 0 for s > 1. In particular f is in I. So J intersect S = I.

Applying this to f = x_i^{N_i}, we get x_i^{N_i} in I for every i. Therefore any monomial x_1^{a_1}...x_d^{a_d} with some a_i >= N_i lies in I, because it is divisible by x_i^{N_i}. So the residue classes of the finitely many monomials
x_1^{a_1}...x_d^{a_d} with 0 <= a_i < N_i for all i
span S/I over k. Hence S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

Therefore the lemma is proved.

payload.statement_nl: Let k be a field, let d be a nonnegative integer, let w_1,...,w_d be positive integers, and let S = k[x_1,...,x_d] with weighted grading deg(x_i)=w_i. Let I be a homogeneous ideal of S. If, over an algebraic closure of k, the common zero locus of I in affine d-space is exactly the origin, then S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space.

result_payload.proof_nl: Let K be an algebraic closure of k, and let J := I K[x_1,...,x_d] inside K[x_1,...,x_d]. The common zero set of I in K^d is the same as the common zero set of J, so by hypothesis V(J) = {0}. If d = 0, then S = k, so I is either 0 or k. If I = k, then J = K and V(J) is empty in K^0, contradicting V(J) = {0}. Hence I = 0, and therefore S/I is isomorphic to k, so it is finite-dimensional over k. Now assume d >= 1. By Hilbert's Nullstellensatz over the algebraically closed field K, the radical of J is the ideal of all polynomials vanishing at the origin, namely (x_1,...,x_d). Therefore, for each i, there exists N_i >= 1 such that x_i^{N_i} belongs to J. We claim that J intersect S = I. The inclusion I subseteq J intersect S is immediate. For the reverse inclusion, let f be in J intersect S. Since f is in J, we can write f = sum_{r=1}^m A_r g_r with A_r in K[x_1,...,x_d] and g_r in I. Let V be the finite-dimensional k-subspace of K spanned by 1 and by all coefficients of all A_r. Choose a k-basis 1 = b_1, b_2, ..., b_t of V. Then each A_r can be written uniquely as A_r = sum_{s=1}^t b_s B_{r,s} with B_{r,s} in S. Hence f = sum_{s=1}^t b_s G_s, where G_s := sum_{r=1}^m B_{r,s} g_r belongs to I. Define H_1 := G_1 - f and H_s := G_s for s > 1. Then sum_{s=1}^t b_s H_s = 0 in K[x_1,...,x_d]. Write H_s = sum_alpha c_{s,alpha} x^alpha with c_{s,alpha} in k. Since the monomials x^alpha are K-linearly independent, for every alpha we have sum_{s=1}^t b_s c_{s,alpha} = 0 in K. Because b_1, ..., b_t are k-linearly independent, all c_{s,alpha} are 0. Thus every H_s = 0, and in particular f = G_1 belongs to I. This proves J intersect S = I. Applying this to x_i^{N_i}, we obtain x_i^{N_i} in I for every i. Therefore any monomial x_1^{a_1} ... x_d^{a_d} with some a_i >= N_i lies in I, because it is divisible by x_i^{N_i}. Hence the residue classes of the finitely many monomials x_1^{a_1} ... x_d^{a_d} with 0 <= a_i < N_i for all i span S/I over k. Therefore S/I is finite-dimensional as a k-vector space. This proves the lemma.
result_payload.proof_summary: Extend scalars to an algebraic closure K and let J be the extended ideal. Nullstellensatz gives radical(J) = (x_1,...,x_d), so some powers x_i^{N_i} lie in J. An explicit coefficient argument shows J intersect S = I. Hence x_i^{N_i} lies in I for every i, so modulo I all monomials with some exponent at least N_i vanish. Only finitely many monomials survive, and their residue classes span S/I over k.
